title: Enums and the match that reads them
summary: Declare the letters once as an enum, then let match map each case to a remark.

blocks.html: src/GradeCalculator.php keeps its letter grades in a table of plain strings: ['min' => 98, 'grade' => 'A+'], and so on down to 'D'. It works. It also has no idea which letters exist, so a typo in that table ships a wrong letter grade to the page and raises no error anywhere.

blocks.title: a string is any string
blocks.code:
<?php

// The letter is a string, so every string is a legal letter grade.
function remarkFor(string $letter): string
{
    if ($letter === 'A') {
        return 'Excellent';
    }

    if ($letter === 'B') {
        return 'Good';
    }

    return 'Unknown letter';
}

echo remarkFor('A'), "\n";
echo remarkFor('a'), "\n";

blocks.html:
'a' is not 'A', so the second call lands in the fallback and nobody hears about it. The type says string, and every string qualifies.

An enum declares the whole set once. You list the cases, and the enum name becomes a real type: a parameter typed Suit accepts Suit::Hearts and nothing else. Each case is one object — there is exactly one Suit::Hearts in the program — so === against a case is always safe.

blocks.title: a pure enum
blocks.code:
<?php

enum Suit
{
    case Hearts;
    case Spades;
    case Clubs;
}

$card = Suit::Hearts;

echo $card->name, "\n";
echo count(Suit::cases()), " cases\n";
var_dump($card === Suit::Hearts);

blocks.html:
That is a pure enum: the cases carry nothing but their names. A backed enum attaches a scalar to every case, which is what you store in a column or a form field: enum Grade: string with case APlus = 'A+';.

->value reads the scalar, Grade::from('A') turns a stored value back into a case, Grade::tryFrom('Z') does the same but returns null instead of failing, and Grade::cases() lists every case in declaration order.

blocks.title: backed enums, values, and lookups
blocks.code:
<?php

enum Grade: string
{
    case APlus = 'A+';
    case A = 'A';
    case F = 'F';
}

echo Grade::APlus->value, "\n";
echo Grade::from('A')->name, "\n";

$missing = Grade::tryFrom('Z');
echo $missing === null ? 'no case for Z' : $missing->value, "\n";

echo count(Grade::cases()), " cases\n";
blocks.output:
A+
A
no case for Z
3 cases

blocks.html: Grade::from() throws a ValueError when the value it is given has no case. Use tryFrom() plus a null check when the value came from a user, a form, or a database row you do not control. The next chapter is about what throwing means.

blocks.html:
Enums can hold methods, so the behavior that used to live in a lookup table can live on the case itself. match is the natural reader: it compares with ===, it never falls through the way switch does, it is an expression that hands back a value, and its arms are tried in the order you wrote them.

If no arm matches and you wrote no default, PHP raises UnhandledMatchError. That is a feature: add a case, and every match that forgot it fails loudly instead of quietly returning the wrong remark.

blocks.title: match reads an enum
blocks.code:
<?php

enum Grade: string
{
    case A = 'A';
    case B = 'B';
    case F = 'F';
}

function remark(Grade $grade): string
{
    return match ($grade) {
        Grade::A => 'Excellent',
        Grade::B => 'Good',
        Grade::F => 'Failed',
    };
}

echo remark(Grade::A), "\n";
echo remark(Grade::B), "\n";
echo remark(Grade::F), "\n";

blocks.title: the tier table rebuilt as an enum
blocks.code:
<?php

use App\GradeCalculator;

enum Grade: string
{
    case APlus = 'A+';
    case A = 'A';
    case AMinus = 'A-';
    case BPlus = 'B+';
    case B = 'B';
    case BMinus = 'B-';
    case CPlus = 'C+';
    case C = 'C';
    case CMinus = 'C-';
    case D = 'D';
    case F = 'F';

    public function minimum(): int
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::APlus => 98,
            self::A => 92,
            self::AMinus => 90,
            self::BPlus => 88,
            self::B => 84,
            self::BMinus => 80,
            self::CPlus => 77,
            self::C => 73,
            self::CMinus => 70,
            self::D => 60,
            self::F => 0,
        };
    }

    public function remark(): string
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::APlus, self::A, self::AMinus => 'Excellent',
            self::BPlus, self::B, self::BMinus => 'Good',
            self::CPlus, self::C, self::CMinus => 'Fair',
            self::D => 'Passed',
            self::F => 'Failed',
        };
    }
}

function letterFor(float $percent): Grade
{
    foreach (Grade::cases() as $tier) {
        if ($percent >= $tier->minimum()) {
            return $tier;
        }
    }

    return Grade::F;
}

foreach ([96.5, 89.0, 74.2, 55.0] as $score) {
    $grade = letterFor($score);
    echo $score, ' -> ', $grade->value, ' (', $grade->remark(), ")\n";
}

$calculator = new GradeCalculator(quiz: 90.0, assignment: 88.0, midterm: 91.5, final: 87.0);
$letter = $calculator->getLetterGrade();
echo 'the project says ', $letter, ', which is ', Grade::from($letter)->remark(), "\n";
blocks.output:
96.5 -> A (Excellent)
89 -> B+ (Good)
74.2 -> C (Fair)
55 -> F (Failed)
the project says B+, which is Good

blocks.title: a case is an object, not a string
blocks.code:
<?php

enum Letter: string
{
    case A = 'A';
    case B = 'B';
}

$grade = Letter::A;

var_dump($grade === Letter::A);
var_dump($grade === 'A');
var_dump($grade->value === 'A');

quiz.q: Which call returns null instead of throwing when the backing value has no case?
quiz.why: tryFrom() returns null for an unknown value. from() throws a ValueError, and cases() takes no argument at all — it just lists every case.

quiz.q: For enum Grade: string { case A = 'A'; }, what does Grade::A->value evaluate to?
quiz.why: ->value is the backing scalar, so it is the plain string 'A'. The case itself stays an object; ->value is how you hand it to anything that stores strings.

quiz.q: A match has five arms and none of them matches the value. What happens?
quiz.why: match has no fallthrough and no silent default: an uncovered value raises UnhandledMatchError, which is how a forgotten enum case announces itself.

exercise.brief: Declare a backed enum Planet: string with the cases Earth = 'earth' and Mars = 'mars'. Print the value of Mars, then print the number of cases on the next line.
exercise.starter:
<?php

enum Planet: string
{
    case Earth = 'earth';
    // add Mars here
}

echo Planet::Mars->value, "\n";
echo count(Planet::cases()), "\n";
exercise.hint: The case syntax is the same as Earth: case Mars = 'mars';. A backed case is always declared with its value, and Planet::cases() returns all of them.
exercise.solution:
<?php

enum Planet: string
{
    case Earth = 'earth';
    case Mars = 'mars';
}

echo Planet::Mars->value, "\n";
echo count(Planet::cases()), "\n";
